newsitem.title: UK: UK's SFA examining roles of NatWest staff.
newsitem.headline: UK's SFA examining roles of NatWest staff.

text.p: UK financial regulator the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) said on Thursday it would be examining the roles of six individuals over the 90 million stg options losses at NatWest Markets.

"We have been notified by NatWest of these additional persons who fall within our remit. We will need to examine their conduct with regard to the recent situation at NatWest," SFA spokesman David Jones told Reuters.

Earlier NatWest said it had suspended a further four senior staff over the interest rate options affair, in addition to its global head of options Neil Dodgson who was suspended when the losses first came to light nearly two weeks ago.

As well as reporting all five to the SFA, NatWest has also notified the SFA of the role of former options trader Kyriacos Papouis, who left the firm in December last year for a job at U.S. investment bank Bear Stearns.
Last week Papouis, who NatWest Markets chief executive said the bank had not yet been able to interview, also resigned from Bear Stearns.

NatWest said those suspended on Thursday were Ian Gaskell, head of Swaps Options Trading for Britain and Europe, Christophe Lanson, global head of rate risk management, Jean-Francois Nguyen, managing director of debt derivatives and Phil Wise, chief administrative officer and formerly senior managing director of capital markets.
It stressed the suspensions were "part of NatWest Market's normal investigation procedure and as such carry no implication of misconduct".
The bank said the initial findings had found no flaws in the models used to calculate valuations of the derivatives in question.

Owen said he was disappointed by the "serious deficiency revealed in the interest rate options area", while Derek Wanless, chief executive of the group, said it was "extremely regrettable that the losses and the mis-pricing have gone undetected for so long".

The second stage of NatWest's inquiry is being undertaken by accountants Coopers & Lybrand and law firm Linklaters & Paines, the two firms called in to help NatWest uncover what went wrong and the total value of the losses.
